title: November FIDE Rating List: Nihal Enters Top 20, Sindarov Leads Gukesh By 72 Points
summary: GM Javokhir Sindarov goes into the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship against reigning champion GM Gukesh Dommaraju with a lead of 72 rating points and 22 places on the November FIDE rating list. The biggest climber near the top of the list was GM Nihal Sarin, whose 2859 performance in the European Club Cup took him up to a career-best world number-19, while a casualty was GM Hans Niemann, who dropped out of the 2700 club after a disappointing U.S. Championship. The women's top-10 rankings stayed unchanged, but the U.S. Women's Championship caused wild swings—IM Alice Lee climbed to 14th and took over as the U.S. women's number-one, IM Carissa Yip dropped 31 points, while winner WIM Rachael Li climbed 50 points. The standout women's performance, however, was by FM Bodhana Sivanandan, who earned the international master title and is the seventh youngest IM, male or female, of all time. Despite a number of top players being in action in October, the rankings at the top were left almost unchanged—GM Wei Yi edged above GM Vincent Keymer into eighth place after a strong showing in the European Club Cup, but has since dipped below the German number-one after three draws in the Chinese League. title: Carlsen Trains With Abdusattorov In Spain Ahead Of Total Chess Debut
summary: GM Magnus Carlsen and GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov have teamed up for a training camp in Spain ahead of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot. Joining them are GM David Howell and Carlsen's longtime coach, GM Peter Heine Nielsen. Carlsen and Abdusattorov will be among 24 players competing in Budapest on November 10–20, testing a format combining fast classical, rapid, and blitz. The tournament is a trial run for the FIDE-approved tour, which launches in 2027 and will crown a World Combined Champion. On Saturday, a post shared on Carlsen’s social media accounts offered a glimpse of the preparations at his holiday home in Spain. The post includes three images that include Howell and Nielsen, along with a video of the two top-10 stars playing blitz together. "Someone brought a chess board into this house," the caption reads.

title: Review: Libiszewski's Chigorin Defence – Calculated Risk against 1.d4 d5 2.c4
summary:
"The Chigorin Defence is an opening that brings back romantic chess memories for me. As a teenager, I played it for a few years. More precisely, between 1999 and 2001, as the Mega Database reminds me with unerring accuracy – a quarter of a century ago!" says Hannes Langrock. He is an editor at a publishing house specialising in fiction and an International Master. He lives in Leipzig and plays for ESV Nickelhütte-Aue. Here he reviews Libiszewski's latest course, which brought back a number of memories. | Photos: ChessBase

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6

Free video samples: Introduction and 3.e3

With this double-edged opening, I played some enjoyable, inspired games, such as the one included below against Malte Markert (then Meyer). Those were days when I played chess with all my heart. So my curiosity was aroused when ChessBase advertised GM Fabien Libiszewski's new opening course. How playable is my "old love", the Chigorin Defence, in 2026? Have modern engines led to entirely new approaches, as they have in so many other openings?

Developing the knight to c6 is, in a sense, positionally suspect, as it blocks Black's own c-pawn. But the knight puts pressure on d4, supports …e7-e5, and …dxc4 can also be an idea. Libiszewski begins with a number of model games to convey what he calls the "Chigorin spirit": active play, tactical ideas and keeping the opponent busy.

The protagonists of these model games are mostly familiar names from Chigorin theory, including two games by Morozevich from the 2000s. But there is also a considerably more recent game, Aronian-Rapport, European Club Cup, Novi Sad 2016 :

3.Nc3 Nf6 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.Nf3

Not a critical test. Apparently, even a world-class player like Levon Aronian can be caught off guard by the Chigorin!

5…e5!

6.dxe5 Bb4 7.Bd2 Nxc3 8.bxc3 Ba5

The pawn on e5 is weak, and Black has sufficient compensation for the pawn. Later, Rapport chased the opposing king across the board and won with an impressive attack. The complete game can be replayed below.

In the heart of the course, the theoretical section, Libiszewski largely follows traditional paths, but there are also surprises, such as the following:

3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.e3 e5 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Bd2 Bxc3 There is no time to retreat the queen. In this opening, Black must play quickly and concretely.

7.Bxc3 exd4 8.Ne2 A highly tactical variation. In the past, Black tried, among other moves, 8…Bg4 9.f3 Bxf3, but this does not work particularly well. Better is 8…Nf6 9.Nxd4 0-0 10.Nb5

And now not 10…Qg5 (165 games), but, as Libiszewski shows, 10…Bg4! (6 games, three of them correspondence games). Black is fine. In the event of 11.f3, Black can offer the bishop with 11…Qg5, and the best lines lead to an engine evaluation of 0.00.

Objectively speaking, however, things are not quite so rosy for Black in every variation. According to Libiszewski, 3.Nf3 is the critical move. After 3…Bg4 play can continue with 4.cxd5 Bxf3 5.gxf3 Qxd5 6.e3 e5 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Bd2 Bxc3 9.bxc3 .

The French grandmaster makes no secret of the fact that, by engine standards, White is better thanks to the bishop pair and the central pawn mass. He shows how Black can nevertheless obtain practical chances – after all, it is not entirely clear where the white king will find safety in the medium term.

Libiszewski briefly discusses a new approach, 3...e6 :

Libiszewski has little sympathy for this move, which is not at all in the Chigorin spirit – Black abandons the typical ideas involving …Bg4 and …e7-e5. However, since 3…e6 is the engines' favourite, he still presents some ideas. Black wants either to play …dxc4 at a favourable moment, for example after 4.g3, or to find another way of solving the problem of the knight on c6 in the medium term. Incidentally, in their Chigorin course published on another platform in 2025, grandmasters Jobava and Basso concentrate on 3…e6 rather than 3…Bg4.

A nice bonus is that Libiszewski also covers 2.Nf3 Nc6 in the theoretical section, since 2.Nf3 is, of course, a common choice for avoiding certain concrete variations after 2.c4.

The knight blocks the c-pawn even though White has not yet offered anything with c2-c4. But the bishop can go to f5 or g4, and Black has some ideas: 3.g3 Bf5 4.Bg2 Nb4 , forcing 5.Na3 , is played at the very highest grandmaster level. 3.Bf4 occurred in one of the games in which I tested Libiszewski's repertoire in online blitz. As recommended by Libiszewski, play continued 3…Bg4 4.e3 e6 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4 , reaching a perfectly playable Ragozin-like position for Black.

Conclusion

In his course The Chigorin Defence: A Practical Weapon Against the Queen's Gambit , French grandmaster Fabien Libiszewski presents an active repertoire for Black against 1.d4 d5 2.c4 . Chigorin players cannot expect objective equality in the critical variations – there is no point in fooling ourselves! Libiszewski openly acknowledges this and shows how Black can seek counterplay and pose practical problems for the opponent even in these lines.

Personally, I believe it makes sense for every ambitious player to have a practically unpleasant opening like the Chigorin in their repertoire. Not as a main system in classical chess, which the opponent can expect and prepare for at leisure, but as a surprise option to keep in reserve and as a weapon in faster time controls. That makes it a calculated risk, since hardly any opponent will be particularly well prepared for it when confronted with it unexpectedly.

The product was provided to the author by ChessBase.

About the author:

Fabien Libiszewski, born in 1984 in Saint-Étienne, is a French chess grandmaster, coach and author.

He earned the grandmaster title in 2009. He reached his peak rating of 2547 in 2016. In the same year, he served as captain of the French national team at the Chess Olympiad in Baku.

Libiszewski remains an active player and has regularly published training courses for ChessBase since 2018, particularly on various opening systems. He also worked as a chess consultant and actor on the feature film "Le Tournoi" in 2015.

title: KazChess Masters: Dubov moves ahead with consecutive wins
summary:
Vokhidov and Lazavik trail by half a point

Daniil Dubov has taken the sole lead at the KazChess Masters in Almaty after scoring consecutive victories in rounds five and six. The Russian grandmaster has collected 4½ points from 6 games and stands half a point ahead of Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Denis Lazavik.

The tournament had initially been led by the Kazakh duo of Edgar Mamedov and Denis Makhnev, who both reached 2½/3 . In Thursday's fourth round, however, Lazavik joined them at the top of the standings by defeating Vokhidov. Co-leaders Mamedov and Makhnev both drew their games, while 14-year-old Mark Smirnov scored his second consecutive victory, this time against Sauat Nurgaliyev.

Rounds five and six brought an unusual coincidence. Both days featured three decisive games, and the winners were exactly the same: the tournament's three highest-rated participants, Mahammad Muradli (2662), Dubov (2654) and Vokhidov (2649).

Round 5 results

Round 6 results

Shamsiddin Vokhidov | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Their routes of the three top seeds to the consecutive victories had been rather different. Muradli had started with two losses and two draws, so his back-to-back wins allowed him to return to a fifty-percent score. Dubov, meanwhile, had collected one win and three draws before his latest successes, which have taken him to an undefeated 4½/6. Vokhidov had a more uneven start, with two wins, a draw and a loss, and has now climbed to 4/6.

Lazavik is the only player other than Dubov to remain undefeated, drawing his games in rounds five and six. The Belarusian GM is now tied for second place with Vokhidov. The early co-leaders Mamedov and Makhnev, meanwhile, have both suffered their first defeats and now stand on 3½/6, one point behind Dubov.

Sunday's seventh round will see all three frontrunners playing with the black pieces. With three rounds remaining, Dubov has a narrow advantage, while the two Kazakh players who set the early pace remain within striking distance.

title: The amazing story of Peter Giannatos and the Charlotte Chess Center
summary:
Twelve years ago, a college student in Charlotte with an economics degree and no business plan asked his local chess community for $10,000 to open a chess club. They gave him $30,000. Today the Charlotte Chess Center teaches 2,500 children a week, runs more rated tournaments than there are days in the year, and hosts Judit Polgar, Peter Leko and Boris Gelfand as camp trainers. Sagar Shah travelled to Charlotte for the Daniel Naroditsky Memorial and sat down with founder Peter Giannatos to understand exactly how it was built. | All photos: Courtesy of Peter Giannatos and the Charlotte Chess Center

Peter Giannatos is a man on a mission. I observed him closely during the Naroditsky Memorial. He is the founder of the Charlotte Chess Center and also the person who made the Daniel Naroditsky Memorial possible. I found in Peter a rare combination of someone who meant business but also cared about the little details. He is extremely action-oriented, yet mindful of the right course of action. Seeing the Charlotte Chess Center grow into one of the biggest academies in the US, and indeed the world, made me curious: what were Peter and his team doing that had made them so successful? This interview is the result of that curiosity.

Sagar Shah (SS): This is one of two centres in Charlotte. How many students are there at the Charlotte Chess Center?

Peter Giannatos (PG): This is our North Center – it just opened a few years ago and serves the north corridor of Charlotte. We have a South Center which we call our main campus, which is a little larger. We teach about 500 students a week in our academy classes between the two facilities. We also have school programmes, where we visit schools – that's about 2,000 kids a week across roughly 60 area school programmes. And then of course we have tournaments and adult members. It's a vibrant, well-rounded chess community: young children learning chess, but also adults who play casually or in tournaments.

The approach road near the South Centre has chess sets outside the premises.

SS: 500 in the academies alone. That's a lot. How did the idea of the Charlotte Chess Center begin? Did you always want to teach chess?

PG: I can't say I necessarily always wanted to teach. But when I was at university I started giving private lessons, and eventually I worked in some school programmes to earn a little money. Of course I loved chess, so it didn't feel like a job.

I was very much involved with chess and playing, but I never thought of it as a business. It wasn't until later, as I approached graduation, that I realised I didn't want to give chess up – and that if I pursued a career outside of chess, I wouldn't be able to devote as much time to it.

SS: What were you studying?

PG: Economics at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. I did finish the degree – but I actually opened the chess centre during my final semester at university. I only had a few credit hours left, so it was manageable.

But I had been organising chess from a very young age. The first event I organised and directed was in 2007. I was in high school, and the objective was to raise money for our high school chess team so we could go to nationals. That was my first step into organising chess.

Then a friend of mine, Gary Newsome, and I decided to start a chess club together that met at a library – Queen City Chess. That was in 2007–08. Once a week, occasionally a weekend tournament, but primarily just a club meeting. We were a community-based chess club like those that exist in many places in the US and I'm sure around the world.

Teaching and organising came naturally to Peter.

SS: And there was no business intention behind that?

PG: None at all. I was involved with it because I wanted to play chess. I was in high school, then just starting college, and I was doing it so I had a place to play. It was all volunteer. It wasn't until late 2013, early 2014 that I understood – okay, my life is changing now. I was initially planning to go into banking. Charlotte is actually known as a financial hub in the US, and that was the most natural course for me to take.

But from 2007 to 2013 we had developed such a great reputation within our community with Queen City Chess. So I thought: could a self-sustaining chess centre work? There weren't many models to go by. But I had some business skills – my family ran businesses when I was a kid, restaurants – and I went to school for business. So I at least had an idea of how it could work.

My thinking at the time was simple: I could do everything. I could run the tournaments, I could teach the classes, I would do anything to make it work. So I put together a business proposal and I approached selected members of our community and asked for contributions to start the Charlotte Chess Center.

Bonnie Cone Center at UNC Charlotte (where Peter graduated from university). Peter used to run his monthly Saturday tournaments there. His events there dated back to 2008, when he was still at high school.

SS: Before we get to that – how strong were you as a player? You're an FM. What were your best achievements?

PG: I started chess late. I played my first tournament as a 13-year-old, in eighth grade, and I was no hidden gem or anything like that. My first US Chess rating was just over 500. So I was not some hidden talent.

But I fell in love with the game, and it consumed me a little bit. I'd say an early achievement was going from a 500-rated player to a 2000-rated player in about three and a half years, which was pretty fast for someone who had just started. But it was only because I loved it. I was immersed in it and studied all the time.

Back then I was playing on FICS – the Free Internet Chess Server, the alternative to ICC.

SS: I heard about FICS just two or three days ago! Everyone in the bughouse community played there.

PG: Yes. It was the Lichess of its time. My friend and I would play league games on FICS. I was totally consumed with chess; I would read every book. Then I became a National Master at 22, and I made the FM title when I was 27. I played a little after that – a couple of tournaments – and then focused my energy on the Charlotte Chess Center. I don't regret that shift, because I feel the impact has been so much greater as an organiser and facilitator of the game than as a player.

Although he didn't become an IM or a GM, Peter's impact towards the game of chess has been huge thanks to his work with the Charlotte Chess Center.

SS: What was it about chess that you liked so much?

PG: It's hard for me to say. I'm a natural competitor – I like a sense of achievement. I'm not sure exactly what was so attractive about chess back then, but once I got into it I was just hungry to compete. I think one attribute of chess I enjoy is that the burden of success and failure falls on the individual. I've always felt comfortable with that. Not that I'm not a team player – I just don't want my flaws to affect so many other people. So team sports were not always accommodating for me as a kid. Chess and tennis became my true life passions, and I still play both today. I'm on the tennis court about ten hours a week – you can probably see it from my tan.

Another of Peter's passions: tennis

"We wanted to raise $10,000; we raised $30,000"

SS: Let's come back to starting the centre. You went to the community and said, I want to start a chess centre – will you contribute? That's a very novel approach.

PG: Queen City Chess had been running from 2007–08 up until that point, so there was at least some trust built in the community. I wasn't, let's say, a fly-by-night operator – somebody just coming through hoping for an opportunity and then leaving. I was very much a part of the community as a player, as somebody who grew up here in Charlotte, and as a facilitator of the game.

So when I asked for contributions, I approached members individually. Here's the plan, here's what we're trying to raise. Our goal was $10,000.

SS: That's not too much.

PG: Not a lot. The idea was a very simple, small club with tables and chairs, where I could manage everything myself. If we grew, fine; we could move into something bigger. But otherwise I was willing to do all the work myself to have a sustainable centre. We just needed some start-up money.

As I approached members individually, they were actually very welcoming to the idea of a dedicated place for chess. And little by little – long story short – through individual members of the community, no companies, nothing like that, we raised $30,000.

SS: Three times your target.

PG: That far exceeded my expectations. All of it went toward the facility, but it meant we could have a nicer facility than we'd planned – tables, chairs, some renovations.

That was the highlight for me, because the community supported it. It wasn't artificial. There was no venture capitalist. They were expecting nothing in return. All they did was trust that I would do it, and they were willing to take a risk on a philanthropic contribution to see what would happen. I hope they're proud now, 12 years later. But back then, it was rolling the dice for them.

SS: And you acknowledged their contribution permanently.

PG: At our South main centre, they're still listed to this day on a plaque on the wall. If we were there, you'd be able to see the original donors from more than 12 years ago.

The people who contributed to making the Charlotte Chess Center possible

SS: What was Charlotte's chess scene like before that?

PG: There was chess in Charlotte, but it was fairly fragmented – and I'd say in most places it's like that. You have your adult faction, and you have youth groups and individuals teaching chess. But there wasn't a place where everybody was welcome.

If you were a child and you went to the adult chess club, maybe they'd say your etiquette isn't good. And the adults would not find a home in a youth chess organisation. So typically most places have this divide between adult or open groups and youth groups. My goal was to bring those groups together – which we were already doing to some degree with Queen City Chess. Our community wasn't huge, but it was vibrant, and it was balanced.

You have to get into my mind back then. It's not like it is now. The pure goal was just to give people a chess home where they could play and learn.

The premises of the Charlotte Chess Center

"If I could turn back time, I would not have done it"

SS: But Queen City Chess was already doing a bit of that. What was the reason to build a physical centre from scratch?

PG: I'll tell you – I noted this in a previous interview with Ben Johnson of Perpetual Chess too. If I could turn back the hands of time, I would have done what you're describing. I would have built it more using common spaces, like the library we were in, and further built out the community before rushing into opening a centre.

Because having these walls, having to pay utilities, having to pay rent, actually takes resources away from the community. It provides opportunity – you have a dedicated space, you have flexibility over when you use it. But back then we were not in a place that warranted a facility, because we didn't have enough people playing and learning chess to justify that overhead. Now it's fully justified. But then it was not.

SS: So you'd call yourself lucky?

PG: Lucky, and maybe a little tenacious – because I was willing to work at no cost. I was following my dream and I wanted to show those who trusted me that I could pull it off.

That $30,000 primarily covered start-up costs. By the time it had run out, we were beginning to see a little revenue – but just enough to cover expenses, not for me to make a living. I was doing it purely out of passion, and I was okay with that.

So if you came into the chess centre back then, I was the one who greeted you at the front desk. I was the one doing the pairings. I was teaching the classes, cleaning the toilets and taking the rubbish out. It was a different time, but I was willing to do that because it was a dream.

My advice to anyone listening who might be interested in doing this: build the community more first. There are ways to build without sinking your resources into physical centres, without fixed costs and recurring expenses weighing on you. Once you reach a certain capacity, then you can start to consider it.

"I was doing it purely out of passion, and I was okay with that"

SS: Your family – didn't they have issues with this? You were an economics graduate, you could have made a very good living at a bank.
